reading.body:
Every tool in this category carries a compliance burden that does not exist for general-purpose AI: patient data, diagnostic liability, and federal regulatory frameworks are embedded in the notes for each entry, not treated as afterthoughts.

Four of the five vendors are US-based and subject to HIPAA, with two entries explicitly flagging the Business Associate Agreement requirement and one noting FDA Software as a Medical Device considerations. Those requirements mean that deploying any of these tools involves legal infrastructure, not just technical integration. The exception is Insilico Medicine, headquartered in Hong Kong, which the data flags for cross-border data flows, a distinct governance problem when the underlying work touches intellectual property and molecular design.

The data covers five tools and says nothing about market share, clinical outcomes, or the compute infrastructure each vendor relies on. It does not indicate which tools are cleared by regulators versus in development. What it does establish is that the regulatory surface area in healthcare AI is unusually wide, and that a HIPAA BAA, genetic privacy law, and FDA oversight can apply simultaneously to a single deployment, before a single inference is served.
